subject: geography
title: US Middle School Geography - Ecosystems and Biomes
subtitle: How climate, living things, energy flow, and human choices shape ecosystems and major world biomes.
description: A source-faithful revision pack on ecosystems, biomes, food webs, climate controls, biodiversity, ecosystem services, and sustainable human-environment choices.

data.targetWord: a community of living things interacting with each other and with nonliving parts of one place

examples.en-GB: A pond, forest, coral reef, or desert can each be studied as an ecosystem.

data.targetWord: a large natural region with a similar climate, plants, animals, and environmental conditions

examples.en-GB: Tropical rainforest, tundra, desert, grassland, and taiga are major world biomes.

data.targetWord: an area with shared features that make it different from nearby or distant places

examples.en-GB: The Amazon Basin is a rainforest region because it shares climate and vegetation features.

data.targetWord: the surroundings in which people, plants, animals, and other living things exist

examples.en-GB: Air, water, land, climate, soil, and living things all form part of an environment.

data.targetWord: the average pattern of weather conditions in a place over a long period

examples.en-GB: Climate helps explain why rainforests, deserts, grasslands, and tundra form in different places.

data.targetWord: short-term conditions in the atmosphere, such as rain, wind, heat, or cloud

examples.en-GB: A cold day in a desert is weather, not proof that the desert climate is cold.

data.targetWord: a living part of an ecosystem, including plants, animals, fungi, and bacteria

examples.en-GB: Grass, mushrooms, rabbits, bacteria, and hawks are all biotic factors.

data.targetWord: a nonliving part of an ecosystem, such as sunlight, water, temperature, soil, or air

examples.en-GB: Sunlight, water, rocks, soil minerals, and temperature are abiotic factors.

data.targetWord: a living thing that makes its own food, usually by using sunlight for photosynthesis

examples.en-GB: Grass, algae, trees, and cacti are producers because they make their own food.

data.targetWord: a living thing that gets energy by eating plants, animals, or other organisms

examples.en-GB: Rabbits, hawks, frogs, foxes, and humans are consumers in food webs.

data.targetWord: an organism that breaks down dead material and returns nutrients to the environment

examples.en-GB: Fungi, bacteria, and worms act as decomposers in many ecosystems.

data.targetWord: a simple pathway showing how energy moves from one organism to another

examples.en-GB: A food chain could show grass, then grasshopper, then frog, then snake, then hawk.

data.targetWord: a network of connected food chains that shows many feeding relationships in an ecosystem

examples.en-GB: Food webs are more realistic because most organisms eat more than one thing.

data.targetWord: the variety of living things found in an ecosystem or region

examples.en-GB: Tropical rainforests and coral reefs have very high biodiversity.

data.targetWord: a feature or behaviour that helps a living thing survive in its environment

examples.en-GB: Cactus spines, camel water storage, and Arctic fox fur are examples of adaptations.

data.targetWord: the largest population an environment can support over time without running out of resources

examples.en-GB: A pond has a carrying capacity because it can support only so many fish.

data.targetWord: the natural home or living place of a plant, animal, or other organism

examples.en-GB: A desert is the habitat of many cacti and water-saving animals.

data.targetWord: a group of living things that can reproduce with one another

examples.en-GB: Grey wolves are a species because members of the group can reproduce together.

data.targetWord: the movement of nutrients through soil, plants, animals, waste, and decomposers

examples.en-GB: Dead leaves break down, nutrients enter soil, and plants absorb them again.

data.targetWord: the clearing of forests, often for farming, roads, mining, settlement, or timber

examples.en-GB: Deforestation can reduce habitat, increase erosion, and affect rivers and local communities.

data.targetWord: the process of land becoming more desert-like because of drought or poor land use

examples.en-GB: Overgrazed grassland can become dry and bare through desertification.

data.targetWord: using resources carefully so present needs are met without harming future needs

examples.en-GB: Replanting trees and limiting harvest levels are examples of sustainability.

data.targetWord: a benefit people receive from nature, such as food, flood control, or water filtering

examples.en-GB: Wetlands provide ecosystem services by filtering water and storing floodwater.

data.targetWord: a hot, wet biome near the Equator with dense vegetation and high biodiversity

examples.en-GB: The Amazon Basin, Congo Basin, and Southeast Asian rainforests are tropical rainforest regions.

data.targetWord: a tropical grassland biome with warm temperatures, seasonal rainfall, grasses, and scattered trees

examples.en-GB: The Serengeti is a savanna ecosystem with grazing animals and predators.

data.targetWord: a biome defined by very low precipitation, with organisms adapted to water shortage

examples.en-GB: The Sahara, Arabian, Sonoran, and Gobi deserts all receive very little precipitation.

data.targetWord: a middle-latitude biome with grasses, fertile soils, moderate rainfall, and few trees

examples.en-GB: The Great Plains, Pampas, and Eurasian Steppe are temperate grassland regions.

data.targetWord: a forest biome with broadleaf trees that lose leaves during winter or a cold season

examples.en-GB: Eastern United States, western Europe, and parts of East Asia contain deciduous forest.

data.targetWord: a high-latitude coniferous forest biome with long cold winters and evergreen trees

examples.en-GB: Taiga forests stretch across Canada, Alaska, Scandinavia, and Siberia.

data.targetWord: a cold biome with low-growing plants, low precipitation, and very short growing seasons

examples.en-GB: Northern Alaska, northern Canada, Greenland edges, and northern Russia contain tundra.

data.targetWord: a biome with hot dry summers, mild wetter winters, shrubs, small trees, and fire-adapted plants

examples.en-GB: Coastal California and the Mediterranean Basin both include this biome.

data.targetWord: a water-based ecosystem, including freshwater rivers and lakes or marine oceans and reefs

examples.en-GB: Streams, wetlands, oceans, estuaries, kelp forests, and coral reefs are aquatic ecosystems.

data.targetWord: a water-rich ecosystem that can filter water, store floodwater, and provide wildlife habitat

examples.en-GB: Wetlands support birds, fish, amphibians, insects, and important flood protection services.

data.targetWord: ground that remains frozen for at least two years in cold environments

examples.en-GB: Thawing permafrost can damage roads, buildings, pipelines, habitats, and travel routes.

data.targetWord: the breaking of a habitat into smaller separated pieces, often by roads or development

examples.en-GB: Habitat fragmentation can make it harder for animals to find food, mates, or migration routes.

data.targetWord: movement from one place to another by people, animals, or other living populations

examples.en-GB: Serengeti grazing animals migrate to follow seasonal rainfall, fresh grass, and water.

data.targetWord: the protection of natural environments, resources, species, and habitats from avoidable damage

examples.en-GB: National parks and protected migration routes are examples of conservation.

data.targetWord: a warm shallow marine ecosystem with high biodiversity and important coastal protection value

examples.en-GB: Coral reefs support fishing, tourism, marine habitats, and many coastal cultures.

data.sentence: A large region with similar climate, plants, and animals is called a ____.
data.hint: It is larger than one ecosystem.
It can change from one day to the next.

data.sentence: A nonliving part of an ecosystem, such as sunlight or water, is an ____ factor.
In most food chains, energy begins with the Sun and enters ecosystems through ____.
A ____ is more realistic than a food chain because it shows many connected feeding relationships.
data.hint: It is a network, not one straight line.

data.sentence: Tropical rainforests are usually found near the ____.
data.hint: This latitude receives strong sunlight throughout the year.

data.sentence: Many deserts form near 30 degrees north and south because sinking air reduces ____ formation.
data.hint: Fewer of these usually means less rainfall.

data.sentence: Ground that remains frozen for at least two years is called ____.
data.hint: It is common in tundra regions.

data.sentence: Clearing forests for farming, roads, mining, or settlement is called ____.
data.hint: It can reduce habitat and expose soil.

data.sentence: Using resources carefully so future people can meet their needs is called ____.
data.hint: It does not mean never using resources.

data.sentence: Wetlands can provide ecosystem services by filtering water, storing floodwater, and providing ____.
data.hint: Animals and plants need this living place.

data.sentence: The Serengeti savanna is known for a major animal ____ linked to seasonal rainfall.
data.hint: Animals move to find fresh grass and water.

data.sentence: The Great Plains became an important farming region partly because temperate grasslands often have fertile ____.
data.hint: Grass roots help build and hold them.

data.sentence: Deserts are defined by low ____, not only by high temperature.
data.hint: This includes rain, snow, sleet, and hail.

data.sentence: A biome map is simplified because real biome borders often blend across ____ zones.
data.hint: Biomes do not have perfectly sharp edges.

data.title: Energy Flow in a Grassland Food Chain
data.instruction: Put the energy flow steps in the correct order.
items: Sunlight provides the original energy source.
Grass uses sunlight to make food through photosynthesis.
A grasshopper eats the grass and gains some of its energy.
A frog eats the grasshopper and gains less available energy.
A hawk eats the snake as a top predator.

data.title: Nutrient Cycle
data.instruction: Put the nutrient cycle steps in the correct order.
items: Dead leaves, waste, and animal remains collect in the ecosystem.
Decomposers break the dead material down.
Plants absorb nutrients from the soil.
Animals eat plants or other animals.
Waste and dead material return nutrients to the cycle.

data.title: How Deforestation Can Affect an Ecosystem
data.instruction: Put the effects of deforestation in a logical order.
items: Forest is cleared for farming, roads, logging, mining, or settlement.
Habitat is reduced or broken into smaller pieces.
Some species lose food, shelter, or migration routes.
Soil is more exposed to heavy rainfall.
Erosion and river sediment can increase, affecting water quality and communities.

data.title: Producer, Consumer, Decomposer, or Abiotic Factor?
data.instruction: Sort each item into the correct ecosystem category.

data.title: Match Features to Biomes
data.instruction: Sort each feature into the biome it best describes.

pairs.text: high rainfall all year and dense tree layers
warm all year with wet and dry seasons
very low precipitation and sparse vegetation
fertile soils often used for grain farming
long cold winters and evergreen conifer trees

data.title: Types of Ecosystem Services
data.instruction: Sort each example into the correct ecosystem service category.

pairs.text: food from farms, fisheries, and forests
fresh water used by people and communities
tourism and recreation in natural areas
spiritual meaning and sense of place
